issues.legal_issue: A liberal, justice-oriented assessment of sufficient cause is required when deciding whether to condone delay in seeking to set aside abatement and substitute a deceased party in a pending appeal.
material_facts: Several appellants in a pending partition appeal died, and applications to substitute some of their heirs were filed after delays ranging from months to years.

The appellants belonged to different families and villages; the affected appellants were rustic and illiterate villagers, and some deceased appellants were transferees living in different areas from the joint-family parties.
After learning of the deaths from counsel, an appellant obtained the heirs’ authorisations and the substitution application was filed promptly.

The respondents did not allege that the delay was mala fide, intentional, or part of a dilatory strategy, and did not deny that the appellants were rustic villagers and, with one exception, illiterate.
The High Court refused to condone the delay and set aside abatement for the affected appellants’ appeals.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in refusing relief. It condoned the delay, set aside abatement, allowed substitution, and remitted the appeal for decision on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “sufficient cause” in Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, Order 22 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and similar provisions should be construed liberally to advance substantial justice where negligence, inaction, or want of bona fides is not imputable to the party. There is no fixed formula: the acceptability of the explanation, rather than the length of delay alone, is the criterion. Courts should ordinarily accept an adequate explanation, while considering any valuable right acquired by the opposing party and balancing the consequences of the decision. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Administrator, Howrah Municipality (1972) 1 SCC 366; Sital Prasad Saxena v. Union of India, AIR 1985 SC 1; Rama Ravalu Gavade v. Sataba Gavadu Gavade (1997) 1 SCC 261; N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy (1998) 7 SCC 123; and Shakuntala Devi Jain v. Kuntal Kumari (1969) 1 SCR 1006.

rule.if: pending_appeal_affected_by_party_death and delayed_substitution_application and parties_are_rural_or_illiterate and prompt_action_after_learning and not intentional_or_mala_fide_delay

predicates.pending_appeal_affected_by_party_death: An appeal was pending when a party to it died, making substitution of that party’s legal representatives relevant to continuing the appeal.
predicates.delayed_substitution_application: The application to substitute the deceased party’s legal representatives was filed after the prescribed time.
predicates.parties_are_rural_or_illiterate: The parties responsible for taking the procedural steps were rural or illiterate litigants.
predicates.prompt_action_after_learning: The litigants took steps promptly after learning of the deaths and receiving advice about the required action.
predicates.intentional_or_mala_fide_delay: The delay was deliberate, mala fide, or part of a dilatory strategy.

issues.definition: When a pending appeal is affected by a party’s death and a late substitution application follows prompt action after the litigants learn of the death, rural or illiterate circumstances, and no intentional or mala fide delay, the delay is condoned and abatement is set aside.
